items.summary: The Radio Shack TRS-80 Colour Computer may never have achieved the sales volume of its competitors from Commodore or Apple, but it offered a surprisingly capable set of hardware. There were three versions, with the final one being a significant upgrade in many ways. There was no upgrade path for owners of version 1 and 2 machines to have a version 3 back in the day, but now thanks to [Felipe Antoniosi] such an upgrade is possible. How? With a Tang Nano 20K FPGA board , of course! The CoCo 3 had a paged memory system for expansion up to 512k, as well as a significantly more capable graphics chip which while compatible with the original Motorola part offered enhanced graphics. The upgrade emulates these, and connects to the CoCo via a set of daughter boards that connect to where the various motherboard chips sat. it offers an HDMI output as well as analog video and enhanced sound capability, bringing the machine firmly into the 21st century. As mods go to classic hardware, this is quite an invasive one. Whether or not you’d prefer to do this to your CoCo is up to you, but ask yourself this, would you have done this had this board been available in the 1980s? Of course you would. Meanwhile should you become bored with the CoCo, it can also be persuaded to emulate an Apple ][ . items.title: Baochip-1x: A Mostly-Open, 22nm SoC for High Assurance Applications
items.summary: For most people, just getting any old microcontroller or system on chip (SoC) from our favorite – or cheapest – vendor is more than good enough. But if you’re really into high assurance computing where every transistor has to be accounted for, you got a bit of a problem. This is basically why [Andrew “Bunnie” Huang] pitched in and had the Baochip-1x produced . This SoC’s design is based heavily on the FPGA-based CPU in the Precursor device , which itself is claimed to be a fully verifiable communicator design. Since it does have an MMU, you can run any software on it that supports the RV32IMAC RISC-V instruction set, with a Coder’s Guide available for those who might feel interested in this SoC, along with the SystemVerilog and Verilog-based sources . In addition to the DIY assembly process, you can even get a physical hardware version, including the ‘Dabao’ evaluation board with a very Raspberry Pi Pico-shaped form factor. Inside this SoC is a single-core, 350 MHz VexRISC-V core, 4 MB resistive RAM (RRAM) and 2 MB of SRAM, along with a whole heap of security-related features. The same Bunnie Huang who developed and then abandoned Chumby? No thanks. Is this the same Baochip that got blown wide open after being the DEF CON badge this year? items.title: The Sextant: Navigating The Old Way
items.summary: Navigation is easy these days, as we’ve entire complex computerized mapping systems and radio-based positioning systems to find ourselves anywhere on Earth. It might seem simple to use GPS these days, even trivial, but billions of dollars are what it took to make that happen. Back in the day, navigation was simpler, and cheaper, using a handheld device and natural objects in space instead of artificial satellites with atomic clocks. Let’s learn about the sextant, and how it did its job. For most of human history, getting lost at sea was a very real way to die. Coastlines can be followed and landmarks recognised, but once the land drops below the horizon, a crew has little more than dead reckoning to go on. You can estimate of speed, heading and elapsed time, but errors pile up the longer you go without a concrete reference as to where you are. When land is out of sight, the sky can offer that very reference point, but you have to be able to measure it accurately enough. That’s where the sextant comes in. It’s a deceptively simple instrument that is, paradoxically, somewhat difficult to understand at a glance. It’s little more than a frame, a pair of mirrors and a small telescope, which lets a navigator measure the angle between a celestial body and the horizon to a tiny fraction of a degree. Take that measurement at the right moment, work through a few tables referencing the detected angle and the time of measurement, and you’ve got your position on the globe. The sextant was predated by the octant, which dates back to the 1730s in implementation—specifically at the hands of John Hadley and Thomas Godfrey, though Isaac Newton had described such a device in unpublished papers sometime earlier. items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.
